It's entirely possible that something like that leak could happen, with a CI double agent or something, and I know that the leak hasn't even occurred yet. But I feel that the reaction from the Foundation felt a bit nonchalant, for an information breach that large. And if I'm thinking of the Novikov self-consistency theory correctly, it's bound to happen anyways.

I'm probably taking into account the popularity of Wikileaks in present time, dunno if it was that big two years ago; I'm just being extremely nitpicky, so I'll novote.

item.title: Keter-level threat!
item.content:encoded:
Hold on a dogbothering second!
If it can theoretically access files from anywhere and any time, think about the mind-bendingly huge memetic hazard this thing presents!
Download copies of that play that makes evil aliens appear on stage or pictures of that restaurant that makes people eat each other! They don't even have to know what they're looking for if you can find SCP files!
And doesn't the simple fact of the Foundation becoming publicly known-of present a massive threat (doesn't it have one of those CK/XK classifications?)
This could easily be a Keter-level threat!

item.content:encoded:
it does say specifically that the process was only repeatedd 20 times.

in addition to that being a woefully in adequete number of trials, it seems like for the foundations purposes it would be very important to note whether the inaccuracies were false positives or false negatives, an in what proportion, because those differant forms of error have radically different implications regarding the 614's capabilities

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded: 20 trials isn't a good sample size, yes, but given that it takes a day to do the trials and that finding out the precise error rate isn't really of the top priority for the Foundation, I think it seems at the very least more believable than having a random sample of 1000.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Perhaps less they only ran it 20 times, and more they ran it 20 times before getting a 'wrong' result?

If I'm wrong with that one though, I agree. 20 isn't enough. At least run it 100 times so you can confirm the statistics, or something. It might be that the one time out of 20 that it was 'wrong' might be the only time out of 100, or even 1000.
Just something to consider in future.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
It's certainly not what I'd pick :P

The point is that it's not presented as a code name. It's just tossed out there, like, oh hey, here's this dude, opus. They called him possum in high school, yup.

I know kids on this site well enough to know that if someone posted an article referencing "Doctor XxW1ngxPr0xX" kids would flip the hell out. Thing is, names like "opus" and "trebuchet" and "blast" and "spazztique Z" and such are just as impossible to take seriously.

The question is, where do we draw the line, and how willing are we to enforce it? I'm tired of seeing silly names around the place, yo.

item.content:encoded:
I was thinking that if such a leak were to happen, then the foundation would either ignore it or try to spread word that it's just fiction, to avoid a Streisand effect. Remember, Wikileaks is not centralized. If the Foundation starts to "take care" of people spreading the leak, then the documents will be seen as more legitimate in people's eyes and people may spread it even more, while before they may have thought it was a hoax.

Also, by your suggestion, I changed SCPgate. I had a creative lapse when I wrote that.
